newsitem.title: USA: Helmsley buried amid talk of reconciliation.
newsitem.headline: Helmsley buried amid talk of reconciliation.

text.p: Renowned investor and dealmaker Harry Helmsley was buried on Tuesday inside a granite mausoleum with stained-glass windows depicting much of the New York City skyline he owned.
The funeral took place as his widow, Leona, and his partners declared something of a truce in their battle for the Helmsley real estate empire.

The partners last year challenged Leona Helmsley's operation of her husband's real estate management company Helmsley-Spear Inc., a complex web of partnerships that includes an estimated 100 million square feet (9.290 million sq metres) in commercial space, 100,000 apartments and 5,000 hotel rooms nationwide.

The Empire State Building, the Helmsley Palace Hotel and the Lincoln building in Manhattan are the pillars of the business, which also extends to Detroit, Chicago, Los Angeles, San Fransisco, Houston and Washington.

Partners Irving Schneider, 76, and Alvin Schwartz, 84, claimed about $6 million in unpaid compensation and questioned personnel and management changes that they contended violated their employment agreements. An arbitration panel has been selected to resolve the partnership conflicts.
The partners, friends of Harry Helmsley for 50 years, charged that the changes were aimed at stripping assets to decrease the value of their option to buy the company on Harry Helmsley's death.
Schneider and Schwartz attended Tuesday's funeral along with about 80 other people. A spokesman for Leona Helmsley said both men have indicated to her that they may want to resolve the dispute.
"Irving Schneider and Alvin Schwartz each called Mrs. Helmsley separately," spokesman Howard Rubenstein said. "They have known each other for many, many years and all of them suffered a great loss.
"These were friendly, courteous discussions and they basically said, 'let's see if we can resolve this situation'".

Harry Helmsley died of pneumonia on Saturday at the age of 87 in Scottsdale, Arizona, with Leona by his side. It was a second marriage for both and they had no children. Mrs. Helmsley's son from a previous marriage died in 1982.

Helmsley was famous not just for the great buildings he bought, but how he bought them. His deals were unique in that they cut across every part of the New York landscape, from commercial to private apartment space, and became a model for how realtors work in sometimes intricate partnerships.
Forbes magazine ranked him as the 67th richest American, putting his net worth at more than $1.7 billion in October 1996.

At the private funeral attended by relatives and associates, Helmsley was buried inside a 30 feet (9 metre) wide and 20 feet (6 metre) deep granite mausoleum among the rolling hills of Woodlawn Cemetery in New York. The monument has stained glass windows with an image in gold, brown and blue of the city skyline.

"Harry Helmsley was always good as his word," said Archibishop Theodore McCarrick of the archdiocese of Newark, New Jersey, a long-time friend who presided over the service. "His great success gave him much joy. He was a self-made man. He had vision and courage and he was not afraid to dream."
Real estate executives said they expected few short-term changes in the management of the Helmsley buildings and some foresaw a negotiated settlement to the legal dispute.

"There is no way of really knowing, but we are dealing here with three people either in their late 70s or early 80s who are all wealthy in their own right," said Mary Ann Tighe, executive managing director of Edward S. Gordon Co.
"Their one great common bond was that they loved Harry Helmsley. They are smart people and they'll figure out some sort of settlement," she said.

In the late 1980s, Harry and Leona Helmsely were indicted in a federal income tax evasion and mail fraud case. Harry Helmsley was ruled unfit to stand trial because of ill health. Mrs. Helmsley, dubbed "the Queen of Mean" during the trial, was convicted and given a 32-month jail sentence and ordered to pay $7.1 million in fines.

Her sentence was later reduced to 21 months because of her husband's ill health. She served 18 months in prison, one month in a Manhattan half-way house and was then confined for two months in her Manhattan penthouse apartment.
